question: How does the cell of a photovoltaic solar panel convert light to electricity?

The cell of a photovoltaic solar panel converts light to electricity through the photovoltaic effect. When photons (light particles) strike the semiconductor material—typically silicon—in the solar cell, they transfer their energy to electrons in the material. If the energy of the photon is sufficient, it can knock an electron loose from its atom, creating an electron-hole pair. 

The solar cell is structured with a p-n junction, where the p-type and n-type semiconductor layers meet. This junction creates an internal electric field. When the electron-hole pairs are generated, the electric field separates the electrons and holes, pushing the electrons toward the n-side and the holes toward the p-side. This separation creates a voltage difference across the cell. 

When an external circuit is connected, the electrons flow from the n-side through the circuit to the p-side, generating an electric current. This current can then be used to power electrical devices.

No mathematical calculations or unit conversions are needed to explain the physical mechanism.

Final answer:
\boxed{photovoltaic effect}

This process is often referred to as the "tauopathy" pathway.
